title: Scenario 2 — City Centre Refurbishment & Demolition
subtitle: Soft strip, partial demolition and refurbishment of a 1960s six-storey building, with façade retention, a pavement gantry and the public walking past the front door.

brief.client: Marchmont Estates plc (city-centre landlord; the neighbouring shops and offices remain occupied)
brief.location: City-centre high street; the public footpath runs directly against the building line, with occupied retail and office premises on both flanks and a narrow rear service lane
description: You are the Site Manager for the principal contractor on the refurbishment of a 1960s six-storey concrete-framed building.

The works include a full soft strip, demolition of a rear two-storey annexe, temporary propping of retained floors, retention of the rear flank wall, a fully sheeted perimeter scaffold with a pavement gantry, and a complete refit.
The public footpath runs tight against the front elevation under a pavement licence, deliveries come through a narrow rear service lane, and laydown space is limited to a small rear yard.
You must plan the construction phase, control demolition and asbestos risk, protect the public and the neighbours, and hand the building over safely.
constraints: Public footpath directly against the building line — protected by a pavement gantry under licence
Occupied shops and offices immediately either side, sharing party walls and the rear lane
Laydown limited to a small rear yard plus the pavement licence area
Deliveries only via a narrow rear service lane shared with the neighbours
Noisy and dusty works restricted to hours agreed with the local authority
keyRisks: Asbestos in a 1960s building — survey, licensed removal and unexpected finds
Structural instability during partial demolition and alteration
Temporary works: propping to retained floors, flank wall retention, pavement gantry
Falling materials and scaffold interface with the public footpath
Fire in a partially stripped building attached to occupied premises
Dust, noise and vibration affecting neighbours and the public
High volumes of strip-out and demolition waste, including hazardous streams

cppProjectDescription: Refurbishment of a 1960s six-storey concrete-framed building in a constrained city-centre location: full soft strip, demolition of a rear two-storey annexe, temporary propping of retained floors, flank wall retention, sheeted perimeter scaffold with pavement gantry, and complete refit. Duration 34 weeks. Public footpath against the building line; neighbouring shops and offices occupied throughout; deliveries via a narrow rear service lane; laydown limited to a small rear yard and the pavement licence area.

phases.title: Project Brief
phases.intro: Understand the building and its constraints before anything is stripped, cut or demolished — in refurbishment, what you don't know is what hurts you.

steps.title: Your project
body: You are Site Manager for the principal contractor on a 34-week, £3.8m refurbishment of a six-storey 1960s building on a busy high street.

The scope includes a full soft strip, demolition of the rear annexe, temporary propping and flank wall retention, a sheeted scaffold with a pavement gantry over the public footpath, and a complete refit.
The shops and offices next door stay open. Shoppers pass within a metre of your hoarding all day. Your only storage is a small rear yard and whatever the pavement licence allows.
Every decision affects safety, legal compliance, programme, cost, quality, the environment, client confidence, morale, enforcement risk and the likelihood of an accident.
keyPoints: A 1960s building means asbestos until a survey proves otherwise
Partial demolition means structural risk — nothing comes out until the engineering says it can
The public and the neighbours are on the other side of your hoarding for 34 weeks

steps.prompt: The pre-construction information arrives, but it contains no refurbishment and demolition asbestos survey and no structural appraisal of the building. The commercial team want the soft strip started next week to 'show early progress'. What do you do?
steps.context: The building dates from 1964. The rear annexe demolition and the propping design both depend on understanding the existing structure.

options.text: Hold all intrusive work. Get the client to commission a refurbishment and demolition asbestos survey for every area to be disturbed, and a structural appraisal to inform the demolition and propping design, before any strip starts.
options.feedback: Correct. A refurbishment and demolition survey is required before any work that disturbs the fabric of a pre-2000 building, and partial demolition cannot be planned without knowing the structure. Two surveys now prevent exposure, collapse and months of delay later.

options.text: Commission the refurbishment and demolition asbestos survey for all six floors now, and programme the structural appraisal for after the soft strip, when the frame is exposed and the engineer can see exactly what they are appraising.
options.feedback: Half right. Exposing the frame does help the engineer — but strip-out gangs remove partitions, ceilings and screeds that can be doing structural work in an altered 1960s building, and the propping design programme starts with the appraisal, not after the strip.

options.text: Rely on the landlord's management asbestos survey from last year, which covers every floor and lists the known ACMs, and brief the strip gangs on its register so they know which materials to leave for the licensed contractor.
options.feedback: A management survey only assesses materials in normal occupation. It does not look inside voids, risers, screeds and ducts — exactly where the strip gangs are going — so its register cannot tell them what they will find.
options.consequence: Strip gangs opened a riser the management survey had never inspected and found suspect lagging; work stopped on two floors for sampling and a late R&D survey, costing a fortnight.

options.text: Start the soft strip on the ground floor next week with the surveyor working a floor ahead of the gangs, so each area is surveyed before it is stripped and the commercial team still get their early progress.
options.feedback: Unsafe. A survey run a floor ahead of the gangs is under programme pressure from day one, leaves no time to plan and notify licensed removal, and puts gangs in a building whose asbestos is still unknown — one of the most common routes to mass exposure and prosecution.
options.criticalFailure: Soft strip planned to start without a refurbishment and demolition asbestos survey
options.consequence: With the surveyor barely a day ahead, a strip gang broke out insulation board ceilings before results returned; six operatives were exposed and HSE served a prohibition notice.

steps.topic: Refurbishment risk — surveys before disturbance
steps.learningNote: Before refurbishment or demolition of any pre-2000 building: a refurbishment and demolition asbestos survey of every area to be disturbed, and a structural appraisal where the structure will be cut, loaded or removed. No survey, no strip.

phases.title: Pre-Construction Planning
phases.intro: Get the duty holders appointed and the right specialists chosen — refurbishment and demolition punish weak appointments harder than new build.

steps.prompt: The client asks you to confirm the CDM 2015 arrangements for this project. Which allocation is correct?
steps.context: Multiple contractors, a design team including a temporary works designer for the propping and façade retention, 34 weeks' duration, around 35 people at peak.

options.text: Client appoints a principal designer and principal contractor in writing; the project is notifiable, so an F10 goes to HSE and is displayed; demolition is planned in writing before it starts; every designer, including the TW designer, has designer duties.
options.feedback: Correct. With more than one contractor the client must make both appointments in writing, the duration and numbers make it notifiable, and demolition or dismantling must be planned and carried out under a written arrangement by competent people.

options.text: Client appoints a principal designer and principal contractor in writing and submits the F10; for the annexe demolition stage the specialist demolition contractor takes over as principal contractor, then hands the site back to us for the refit and fit-out.
options.feedback: The appointments and the F10 are right, but there is one principal contractor controlling the construction phase. Handing control to the demolition firm mid-project — at the highest-risk stage, with propping, gantry and asbestos all live — is exactly when coordination fails.
options.consequence: At the handback the two firms' permit systems overlapped; a services gang entered the annexe exclusion zone on the wrong permit and was turned out by the machine operator mid-lift.

options.text: Client appoints the principal designer and principal contractor in writing, but holds the F10 until the refit, as the strip and demolition gangs alone won't exceed twenty workers on site at any one time.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Notification is for the project, not a stage — it goes to HSE before the construction phase starts — and with 34 weeks and around 35 people at peak this project exceeds the thresholds however the gangs are counted. Refurbishment, strip-out and demolition are all construction work.
options.consequence: An HSE inspector visiting after a neighbour complaint found no F10 for a notifiable project; the material breach brought a fee-for-intervention invoice and a follow-up visit.

options.text: Let the strip gangs start on the upper floors under the client's letter of intent while the appointment documents are signed — the PD and PC are agreed in principle, and the F10 can name them once executed.
options.feedback: Unsafe. 'Agreed in principle' is not an appointment. Until the client appoints in writing, no one is properly controlling the construction phase — and soft strip in a 1960s building beside occupied neighbours is not low risk.
options.criticalFailure: Strip-out started without CDM duty holders formally appointed
options.consequence: With nobody formally in control, strip gangs worked without induction or a plan; an operative fell through an unprotected riser opening and fractured his leg, and HSE stopped the strip.

steps.topic: CDM 2015 — duty holders, notification and demolition planning
steps.learningNote: Client appoints PD and PC in writing where there is more than one contractor; F10 where thresholds are met; and demolition must be planned in writing by competent people before it begins. Temporary works designers are designers under CDM.

cppText.best: Client: Marchmont Estates plc. Principal Designer and Principal Contractor appointed in writing; F10 submitted and displayed. Temporary works designer engaged for propping, flank wall retention and gantry. Demolition planned in writing by competent persons before work begins.
cppText.partial: Duty holders identified; appointment and demolition planning evidence incomplete.
cppText.poor: Duty holder arrangements unclear — control of the construction phase not established.
cppText.unsafe: Works commenced before duty holders appointed — non-compliant.

steps.prompt: You are selecting the demolition contractor and the asbestos removal contractor. How do you assess them?

options.text: Check the asbestos contractor's valid HSE licence and enforcement history, and assess both firms' experience, training, supervision and RAMS for this job — including the demolition firm's record of engineered sequences beside retained structure.
options.feedback: Correct. Licensable asbestos work may only be done by a licensed contractor, and demolition beside retained structure and occupied neighbours demands demonstrated capability, not just a trade name.

options.text: Shortlist the two lowest compliant tenders, confirm both firms hold the licences and insurances their trades require, and leave method to the post-contract RAMS review, since detailed sequencing is the demolition engineer's responsibility anyway.
options.feedback: Licences and insurance set a floor, not a guarantee, and leaving capability to the post-contract RAMS means discovering a weak firm after you have appointed it. The cheapest demolition price is often bought by cutting the engineering, the sequence or the supervision.
options.consequence: The cheapest demolition firm's supervisor had never worked to an engineered sequence; their RAMS was rejected three times and the annexe demolition started three weeks late.

options.text: Accept the firms' SSIP and trade-association accreditations as the competence check, since those schemes already audit training records, insurance and safety policies, and collect CSCS card copies at induction.
options.feedback: Accreditation is a useful starting point, but it audits a firm's systems, not whether it can prop, sequence and drop this annexe next to this retained wall. Project-specific capability has to be tested before appointment.
options.consequence: The accredited demolition firm proposed an excavator too heavy for the back-propped slabs; the mismatch surfaced at RAMS review and forced a plant change and two weeks' delay.

options.text: Award the insulation board removal to the strip-out contractor as a variation — their operatives hold asbestos awareness and non-licensed work training, it avoids a second firm on the floors, and keeps one gang accountable.
options.feedback: Unsafe and unlawful. Neither awareness nor non-licensed work training permits removal of asbestos insulation board on this scale — that is licensable work for an HSE-licensed contractor, notified in advance and carried out under enclosure.
options.criticalFailure: Licensable asbestos removal assigned to an unlicensed contractor
options.consequence: Strip operatives broke out insulation board ceilings with no enclosure; fibre migrated down the stairwell, two floors were contaminated, and HSE served a prohibition notice and later prosecuted.

steps.topic: Competence — licensed asbestos work and demolition capability
steps.learningNote: Match the check to the risk: HSE licence and notification history for the asbestos contractor; engineered-sequence demolition experience, trained operatives and strong RAMS for the demolition contractor. Awareness training only teaches people to avoid asbestos, never to work on it.

cppText.best: Asbestos removal by HSE-licensed contractor (licence verified). Demolition contractor assessed for engineered partial-demolition capability. All operatives inducted; asbestos awareness training for all trades; demolition, scaffold and TW roles competence-verified; training records held on site.
cppText.partial: Competence checks partially complete; gaps to close before demolition and asbestos removal.
cppText.poor: Appointments made on cost and accreditation logos alone.
cppText.unsafe: Licensable asbestos work allocated to unlicensed contractor — non-compliant.

steps.prompt: Put these pre-construction activities in the order they must happen, from appointment through to the first high-risk work on site.
steps.context: Several items can run in parallel; what matters is that nothing starts before the information or approval it depends on.

activities.label: Client appoints PD and PC in writing; F10 to HSE
activities.detail: More than one contractor and a notifiable project: both appointments and the notification come first.

activities.label: Refurbishment & demolition asbestos survey
activities.detail: Every area to be disturbed, including voids, risers, screeds and the annexe.

activities.label: Structural appraisal of the 1960s frame
activities.detail: Informs the demolition sequence, the propping and the flank wall retention design.

activities.label: Appoint licensed asbestos and demolition contractors
activities.detail: HSE licence verified; demolition firm assessed for engineered work beside retained structure.

activities.label: TW designs produced and independently checked
activities.detail: Propping and gantry at cat 2, flank wall retention at cat 3, against the TWC's design brief.

activities.label: Construction phase plan and demolition plan in place
activities.detail: Covers welfare, fire, emergency, public protection, the asbestos sequence and demolition arrangements.

activities.label: Mobilise: hoarding, gantry, welfare, lane logistics
activities.detail: Gantry erected to the checked design and loaded only after the TWC's permit to load.

activities.label: First high-risk work: licensed asbestos removal
activities.detail: Notified to the regulator in advance, enclosures and decontamination unit set up.

constraints.reason: The principal contractor drafts the construction phase plan, so it must be appointed first.
The survey defines the licensable asbestos scope the removal contractor is assessed and appointed for.
The plan's asbestos sequence and strip arrangements depend on knowing what the survey found.
Propping and retention cannot be designed without knowing how the existing structure carries load.
The written demolition arrangements in the plan must be built on the structural appraisal.
Erecting the pavement gantry over a live footpath before its design is checked puts the public under an unverified structure.
The construction phase must not start until a suitable construction phase plan is in place.
Licensable work may only be carried out by the licensed contractor once appointed and notified.
Hoarding, welfare and the lane controls must be in place before high-risk work starts.
Intrusive work before the R&D survey risks disturbing asbestos nobody has identified.

steps.topic: Pre-construction sequencing — CDM 2015 appointments, surveys and TW design
steps.learningNote: Information before design, design before construction, approval before use. The R&D survey and structural appraisal feed the contractor selection, the temporary works design and the construction phase plan — and the construction phase, starting with mobilisation, cannot begin until those are in place.

phases.title: Construction Phase Plan
phases.intro: The construction phase plan must be written for this building — asbestos, demolition sequence, propping, the gantry and the neighbours — and it must exist before anyone starts.

steps.prompt: The client wants the strip gangs in on the 1st of the month. Your construction phase plan is drafted, but the asbestos removal sequence, the fire plan for the stripped building and the demolition arrangements are incomplete. Can the construction phase start?

options.text: No. Complete the plan so far as reasonably practicable for the works being done — welfare, emergency and fire arrangements, public protection and the asbestos sequence — before anyone starts, and develop the demolition detail before that stage.
options.feedback: Correct. The construction phase must not start until a suitable plan is in place for the work being carried out. The demolition sections can mature later — the day-one arrangements cannot.

options.text: Start on the 1st with enabling works only — hoarding, welfare and gantry foundations — under a short interim plan covering those tasks, and complete the asbestos, fire and demolition sections in the first week.
options.feedback: Defensible only if the interim plan genuinely covers the enabling works being done — and welfare, fire and emergency arrangements are needed from the first day, not the fifth. The strip itself must wait for the full asbestos and fire sections.

options.text: Issue the company's standard refurbishment plan template for day one — it already covers asbestos, demolition, fire and temporary works in general terms — and add the building-specific detail as each trade's RAMS arrive over the first month on site.
options.feedback: A plan that doesn't describe this building's asbestos, propping, gantry or neighbours won't control any of them, and adding detail 'as the RAMS arrive' lets the trades write your plan. Inspectors read the first three pages and know.
options.consequence: The template said nothing about fire in the stripped floors; a waste fire in a fifth-floor bay found no temporary alarm or waste regime, and the clean-up and investigation lost four days.

options.text: Start on the 1st as the client wants, finish the plan during the first fortnight, and issue it showing the start date on the cover so the document set reads as continuous if the client's auditor or HSE ask.
options.feedback: Never falsify safety documents. Dating a plan to before it existed is a serious breach that destroys your credibility and any legal defence — and the works it should have controlled ran uncontrolled in the meantime.
options.criticalFailure: Considered backdating the construction phase plan
options.consequence: An operative fell through an unguarded stair void in the first week; HSE's investigation found the plan's cover date preceded its drafting, and the falsified record led to prosecution.

steps.topic: CDM 2015 — construction phase plan for refurbishment and demolition
steps.learningNote: The CPP must be in place before the construction phase begins and must actually address this project's principal risks: asbestos, structural instability, temporary works, fire in a stripped building and the public interface. It is a live document — the demolition sections must be complete before demolition starts.

cppText.best: Site rules set before mobilisation: induction mandatory; permits enforced (hot works, demolition, loading, isolation); no entry to asbestos-controlled or demolition exclusion areas; no alteration of props or scaffold; deliveries booked via rear lane only; agreed noisy-works hours observed; daily waste removal; PPE and housekeeping standards; neighbour consideration rules.
cppText.partial: Interim site rules issued; full set completed during week one.
cppText.poor: Generic site rules not tailored to demolition, asbestos or the public interface.
cppText.unsafe: No effective site rules at start of construction phase.

phases.title: Site Set-Up
phases.intro: Lay out a site with almost no space. The public footpath and gantry are at the front, the neighbours are either side, and everything else must work from the small rear yard and the service lane.

steps.prompt: Place the site set-up items. The high street and footpath run along the top — the gantry protects the footpath in front of the building. The building fills the centre with occupied neighbours either side. The rear annexe (to be demolished), the small yard, the service lane and a surface water drain are at the back. Place every required item where it is safest and most practical.

rules.placementNote: Hoarding on the licensed pavement strip and across the rear yard boundary keeps the public and lane users out of the works.
The only vehicle gate is off the rear service lane — never through the high-street frontage.
A separate pedestrian gate off the lane so operatives never enter with vehicles.
Statutory signage at the gate, plus public information on the hoarding and gantry.
A marked route from the gate to welfare and the building entrance, clear of the demolition zone and vehicle standing area.
Deliveries come along the lane into the yard, marshalled — never over the footpath.
A marshal controls the shared lane at the gate — the neighbours' vehicles and pedestrians use it too.
Stacked welfare units in the yard, or an early-established ground-floor welfare area kept clear of strip works — never in the demolition zone or blocking the lane.
Toilets and washing with the welfare, connected and maintained.
Site office and induction room by the gate route, where everyone passes it.
First aid point at welfare, signed, with trauma provision for demolition works.
Fire points at the building exits and stair cores — escape routes through a stripped building must stay protected.
Muster in the lane or open yard, agreed with the neighbours, clear of the building and the demolition zone.
Segregated skips in the yard — a skip in the lane blocks the neighbours' access and the fire brigade.
Laydown is tiny — just-in-time deliveries, with what must be stored kept in the yard.
Gas bottles for hot works live in a locked external cage in the yard, never inside the stripped building overnight.
Sheeted perimeter scaffold on the retained building, founded through the gantry at the front.
A hard exclusion zone around the annexe demolition — nobody inside it while the machine works.
The gantry and fans protect the footpath from falling material — the single most important protection on this site.
Water suppression at the demolition face and the loading point, before dust reaches the neighbours.
Acoustic screens and a noise monitor between the demolition and the occupied offices.
Protect the lane drain from silt-laden water and washdown.

steps.topic: Constrained city-centre site set-up
steps.learningNote: On a tight urban site the set-up is mostly about interfaces: gantry and hoarding between the works and the public, a marshalled gate on the shared lane, welfare and storage squeezed into the yard or the building, gas and waste never left where they threaten escape routes or neighbours.

steps.prompt: Deliveries and muck-away must use the narrow rear service lane, which the neighbouring shop and offices also use for their own deliveries and as a fire escape discharge. How do you manage it?

options.text: Booked delivery slots agreed with the neighbours, a trained marshal controlling every movement in the lane, no waiting on the high street, fire escape discharges kept clear at all times, and reversing designed out or controlled by a banksman.
options.feedback: Correct. A shared lane with pedestrians, neighbour deliveries and fire escapes is a live traffic interface — it needs positive control and cooperation, not first-come-first-served.

options.text: Sign the lane at both ends for construction traffic, issue every haulier a lane plan marking the neighbours' fire exits and loading doors, and ask drivers to give way to neighbour deliveries and pedestrians, with the gateman logging each one in.
options.feedback: Signs and a lane plan help, but they don't marshal a 26-tonne grab lorry past a shop's fire escape. The lane needs a booking system and a trained marshal controlling each movement, not just well-informed drivers.

options.text: Take the bulk deliveries at the front instead, offloading from the high street loading bay across the footpath with a labourer holding pedestrians, and keep the rear lane for muck-away so the neighbours see fewer vehicles.
options.feedback: Offloading across a live city footpath outside your licence conditions, with a labourer holding back shoppers, puts the public directly under the work — and will bring the highway authority to your gate.
options.consequence: A pallet of plasterboard slid off a tail-lift onto the footpath, missing a shopper by a metre; the highway authority suspended front loading until a revised logistics plan was approved.

options.text: Run deliveries first come, first served, with wagons holding in the high street loading bay with hazards on until the lane clears and the driver phoning the gate — it keeps the lane free for the neighbours.
options.feedback: Holding heavy vehicles on a live high street beside a busy footpath, then turning them into the lane unplanned and unmarshalled, creates a hazard for everyone and invites immediate enforcement.
options.criticalFailure: Uncontrolled construction traffic on the live high street
options.consequence: A muck-away wagon held on the high street swung into the lane unmarshalled and struck a cyclist at the junction; the rider was hospitalised and the police and council attended.

steps.topic: Traffic management on a shared urban interface
steps.learningNote: Plan urban logistics as a high-risk activity: booked slots, marshalled movements, no public-road queuing, fire escapes and neighbour access sacrosanct, reversing designed out. The lane is shared space — you control your use of it, not the lane itself.

cppText.best: All vehicles via rear service lane under booked slots; trained marshal controls every movement; no waiting or queuing on the high street; neighbours' access and fire escape discharges maintained at all times; reversing eliminated or banksman-controlled; delivery plan agreed with neighbours and reviewed weekly.
cppText.partial: Lane deliveries signed; marshalling and booking arrangements to be formalised.
cppText.poor: Deliveries taken over the public footpath without agreed control.
cppText.unsafe: Construction vehicles queuing on the live high street.

phases.title: Welfare and Access
phases.intro: Welfare is a day-one duty even when there's nowhere obvious to put it — and on this site, emergency arrangements have to work for a stripped building and the neighbours too.

steps.prompt: The rear yard barely fits the skips and the gas cage. Where does compliant welfare go from day one?

options.text: Double-stacked serviced units in the yard, or a welfare area on the ground floor — surveyed, cleared and separated from strip works — with toilets, warm washing water, drying, rest and drinking water from the first day.
options.feedback: Correct. Constrained sites stack units or use the building itself. What never changes is the standard: full welfare from day one, kept clean and clear of dust and strip operations.

options.text: Agree with the client's facilities manager that operatives use the shopping arcade's toilets and food court for the first month, with a site van carrying drinking water and a hand-wash, until stacked units fit in the yard.
options.feedback: Public facilities you don't control are not compliant provision, and a van with a hand-wash is not washing, drying or rest facilities. Welfare complaints are one of the fastest routes to an inspector's visit on urban sites.
options.consequence: The arcade withdrew access after operatives in dusty workwear used the food court; a welfare complaint reached HSE and the site lost two days setting up emergency units.

options.text: Place a chemical toilet and a hand-wash station in the yard for the first fortnight and use the site cabin as the rest area, then move into the cleared ground floor once the strip has created the space.
options.feedback: Inadequate. Warm washing water, drying, a proper rest area and drinking water are needed alongside toilets from day one — and dusty strip work makes washing provision more important, not less.
options.consequence: Operatives eating in a dusty cabin with a cold-water hand-wash raised a grievance; the strip gang stood down for a day and a follow-up complaint brought an HSE welfare visit.

options.text: Hold the start date back a fortnight, accept the programme loss, and only mobilise once the yard has been reorganised to take full single-storey units for toilets, washing, drying and rest.
options.feedback: Compliant but avoidable — stacking the units, or establishing welfare on a cleared ground-floor area, would have given the same standard from day one without losing a fortnight.

steps.topic: Welfare on constrained sites
steps.learningNote: Space pressure never dilutes Schedule 2: toilets, warm washing water, drinking water, rest, drying and changing from day one. On tight sites, stack units, use the building, or negotiate space — the standard is fixed, only the solution flexes.

cppText.best: Welfare from day one: stacked serviced units in rear yard / cleared ground-floor welfare area with toilets, warm washing water, drinking water, heated rest room, drying and changing. Separated from strip and demolition dust; cleaned daily; sized for peak workforce of 35.
cppText.partial: Interim welfare in place; full provision completed in week one.
cppText.poor: Welfare relies on facilities outside the site's control.
cppText.unsafe: No compliant welfare at start of works.

steps.prompt: Set the emergency arrangements for this project.

options.text: Plan for fire in the part-stripped building, collapse, asbestos release, scaffold or gantry rescue and a frontage incident, with escape kept from every working floor, first aiders each shift, a muster point shared with the neighbours and fire service access via the lane.
options.feedback: Correct. In refurbishment the emergencies to plan for are the building's: fire with compromised compartmentation, collapse, and asbestos release. The plan must also work for the people next door.

options.text: Use the building's existing fire alarm, which is still connected and tested, with first aid kits on each floor, an appointed person on every shift and a 999 procedure at the gate, adding collapse and asbestos scenarios before demolition.
options.feedback: A start, but the existing alarm will be progressively stripped and isolated — you need a temporary alarm that survives the strip — first aid needs assessing for the risks, and collapse and asbestos scenarios are needed from the first day of strip, not just demolition.

options.text: During the demolition period the demolition contractor's emergency procedures govern the whole site, since they hold the collapse and rescue expertise, and the site-wide plan resumes once the annexe is down.
options.feedback: Their procedures cover their work. Fire, collapse and public incidents involve the whole site, the gantry and the neighbours — the principal contractor owns that plan throughout, drawing on the specialist's input.
options.consequence: When strip waste caught fire during the demolition, nobody knew whose procedure applied; the neighbours weren't warned and the fire service found the lane blocked by a skip.

options.text: Keep the existing building evacuation procedure through the strip, with extinguishers on each floor, and write the full project emergency plan once the strip is complete and the layout stops changing every week.
options.feedback: The strip period is the highest fire-load, most changeable phase of the whole job — waste, hot works, escape routes moving every week. An occupancy evacuation procedure doesn't fit it, and that is when the plan is needed most.
options.criticalFailure: No emergency arrangements during the strip-out phase
options.consequence: A waste fire on the fourth floor spread smoke through opened risers; with escape routes changed and no temporary alarm, two operatives were treated for smoke inhalation and the neighbours evacuated.

steps.topic: Emergency planning in occupied-adjacent refurbishment
steps.learningNote: Plan for the building's real emergencies: fire with stripped compartmentation, structural collapse during demolition, asbestos release, rescue from the scaffold. Keep escape routes live as floors change, test the temporary alarm weekly, and coordinate with the neighbours who share your walls.

cppText.best: Emergency plan covers fire in stripped building, structural collapse, asbestos release, scaffold/gantry rescue and public incident at frontage. Temporary fire alarm tested weekly; escape routes reviewed at every floor change; named first aiders every shift; muster point agreed with neighbours; fire service access via lane maintained; neighbour emergency contacts exchanged.
cppText.partial: Basic first aid and alarm arrangements; collapse and asbestos scenarios to be added before demolition.
cppText.poor: Emergency planning delegated to individual contractors.

phases.title: Hazard Identification
phases.intro: Walk the building before the gangs do. In refurbishment and demolition, the killers are the structure, the asbestos, the fire load and the public on the other side of the hoarding.

steps.prompt: Walk the building before the morning briefing. Flag every observation that needs action before work carries on — and leave the ones that are under control. Read each one: they look alike.
steps.location: Site walk-round — strip under way on floors 2–5, annexe demolition being prepared, Tuesday 07:40

observations.text: Ground floor below the skid-steer route: back-props at the drawing positions, each tagged with a permit-to-load number.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. Back-propping for plant on the suspended slabs is a designed, category 2 item; props matching the layout and carrying the TWC's permit-to-load show the hold point has been passed.

observations.text: Rear lane: a grab lorry reversing towards the gate, no marshal in the lane, a neighbour's delivery van waiting behind.
observations.explanation: Hazard. An unmarshalled reversing HGV in a shared lane with pedestrians and fire exit discharges risks a fatal strike. Stop the movement; every lane movement needs the trained marshal and a booked slot.

observations.text: Third floor: blockwork cut with water fed to the blade; the operative is clean-shaven, in a tight-fitting mask.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. Water suppression at the point of cutting controls respirable silica at source, and a tight-fitting mask on a clean-shaven face, backed by a face-fit test on record, is the right second layer.

observations.text: Fourth lift, front elevation: two scaffold ties taken out at stripped window openings; the sheeting is still fixed.
observations.explanation: Hazard. A sheeted scaffold relies on its tie pattern to resist wind load; removing ties while the sheeting stays on risks the scaffold pulling away over the gantry and footpath. Stop use, reinstate to the design, TWC and scaffold inspection before use.

observations.text: Floor two: strip gang removing partitions; a certificate of reoccupation for that floor is posted on the stair door.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. The analyst's certificate of reoccupation after four-stage clearance is the re-entry permit for an area where licensed asbestos removal has taken place — strip following clearance is the planned sequence.

observations.text: Second floor: one prop in the propping layout has its pin replaced with a bent length of rebar.
observations.explanation: Hazard. A proprietary prop is only rated with its own pin; improvised rebar can bend or shear and drop the floor it supports. Clear the bays above and below, TWC and designer to direct a like-for-like replacement, and find out who altered it.

observations.text: Third-floor loading bay: the gate is wedged open with a scaffold board while a pallet sits on the platform.
observations.explanation: Hazard. A loading bay gate held open leaves an unprotected edge three storeys above the lane and lets materials be pushed off the platform. Close the gate; loading bay gates stay shut except during a controlled lift.

observations.text: Retained flank wall: monitoring targets on the brickwork; today's reading in the TW file is inside the green trigger.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. Movement monitoring read to schedule and recorded against defined trigger levels is exactly what lets the TWC and retention designer confirm the cat 3 scheme is behaving as designed.

observations.text: Main stair, second-floor half-landing: six bags of strip waste stacked against the wall waiting for the chute.
observations.explanation: Hazard. Combustible waste on an escape stair is both a fire load and an obstruction on the route out of a part-stripped building. Clear it now; waste goes from the floor to the chute or skip daily and is never staged on stairs.

observations.text: Gantry deck: two pallets of plasterboard; the load notice at the gantry access stair gives a four-pallet limit.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. The gantry deck is a designed loading area with a displayed limit; materials stored within that limit, as notice-boarded, are within the design case. The hazard would be loading beyond it.

observations.text: Fifth floor: a fitter gas-cutting old pipework; hot work permit on display, fire watch standing by with an extinguisher.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. Hot works under a permit with a dedicated fire watch and extinguisher at hand is the planned control; the permit should also show the post-work fire check time before the area is left.

observations.text: Floor four: an operative lifting ceiling tiles in a bay that the survey plan on the wall marks as 'not accessed'.
observations.explanation: Hazard. An area the R&D survey did not access must be presumed to contain asbestos until it has been surveyed. Stop, withdraw, seal the bay and get it surveyed and sampled before any intrusive work.

observations.text: Rear lane: a delivery unloading in its booked slot, the marshal holding pedestrians at the lane mouth.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. Booked slots plus a trained marshal controlling pedestrians and the vehicle is the lane traffic plan working as intended, with the neighbours' access kept clear.

observations.text: First-floor corridor: an extension lead runs across the walking route, taped down at one end only.
observations.explanation: Hazard. A trailing lead across a busy route is a trip risk and gets damaged by trolleys. Re-route it at high level or along the wall edge, or use a cable protector across the route.

observations.text: Third-floor loading bay: up-and-over gate closed, SWL sign fixed at the platform edge.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. A closed up-and-over gate keeps edge protection in place at all times, and the displayed safe working load (SWL) tells the gang what the cat 1 platform was designed for.

observations.text: Second lift: an operative dry-cutting blockwork with a disc cutter; dust drifting out through the sheeting.
observations.explanation: Hazard. Dry cutting creates high respirable silica exposure for the operative and visible dust over the gantry onto the public. Stop; restart only with water suppression or on-tool extraction and face-fit-tested RPE.

steps.topic: Hazard identification — refurbishment walk-round and temporary works condition
steps.learningNote: A walk-round is about reading the detail: the same subject — props, loading bay, lane, cutting, asbestos — can be under control in one bay and dangerous in the next. Look for evidence that the hold point, permit or clearance has been passed, and act on the ones where it hasn't.

steps.prompt: Which set of hazards should be treated as this project's principal risks?

options.text: Structural instability during demolition and alteration; asbestos disturbance; fire in the partially stripped building; falling materials onto the footpath and neighbours; scaffold and gantry failure; live and unknown building services.
options.feedback: Correct. These are the credible multiple-fatality risks on this project — and several of them threaten people outside your hoarding, which raises the stakes further.

options.text: Slips and trips on strip debris, manual handling of plasterboard and waste, hand-arm vibration from breakers and cuts from sheet materials — the injuries that actually fill refurbishment accident books — with asbestos covered by the survey.
options.feedback: All real and all needing management — but frequency isn't severity, and a survey does not control asbestos on its own. Your planning priority goes to collapse, asbestos, fire and the public.

options.text: Collate the significant hazards from each specialist's RAMS — demolition, asbestos, scaffold and strip — into one project register, as each firm has assessed its own trade in far more depth than the PC could.
options.feedback: Collating trade RAMS misses the interfaces no single contractor sees: strip weakening what demolition relies on, hot works near strip waste, demolition vibration on the retained wall, debris over the gantry. Identifying those is the principal contractor's job.
options.consequence: No trade RAMS covered hot works next to strip waste; a cutting spark ignited a waste pile on the third floor, and the floor was evacuated before the fire was put out.

options.text: Dust, noise and vibration affecting the occupied offices, shops and footpath, because neighbour complaints can halt the works through the council and will dominate the project's relationship with the client.
options.feedback: Complaints are the loudest issue, not the most dangerous one. Manage them in parallel — but collapse, asbestos, fire and falling material onto the public come first.
options.consequence: With planning effort spent on nuisance, the gantry fan detail was never reviewed; a scaffold fitting fell past it onto the kerb, narrowly missing a pedestrian.

steps.topic: Principal risks in refurbishment and demolition
steps.learningNote: Refurbishment kills differently from new build: unplanned collapse, asbestos, fire in stripped buildings and falling material onto the public lead the list. Rank by severity and credibility, then plan each named risk specifically.

cppText.best: Principal risks: structural instability during demolition/alteration; asbestos disturbance; fire in partially stripped building; falling material onto footpath/neighbours; scaffold and gantry integrity; live and unknown services. Each carries specific RAMS, engineered controls, exclusion zones and named supervision. Frequent-injury risks (slips/trips, manual handling, HAVS, dust, noise) managed through housekeeping, rotation, monitoring and health surveillance.
cppText.partial: Main risks identified; interface risks between strip, demolition and temporary works need development.
cppText.poor: Risk identification left to individual contractors.
cppText.unsafe: No structured hazard identification for the project.

riskEntry.hazard: Structural collapse / asbestos / fire / falling material onto the public
riskEntry.control: Engineered demolition sequence, licensed asbestos removal, refurbishment fire plan and gantry protection — coordinated by the PC

steps.prompt: The strip will generate large volumes of combustible waste, hot works are needed for cutting out services, and the building's compartmentation will be progressively opened up — all attached to occupied premises. What is your fire strategy?

options.text: Hot work permits with fire watch and post-work checks; strip waste cleared daily, never stored on stairs or in the lane; a temporary alarm kept working through the strip; escape routes reviewed at each change; compartmentation kept as long as possible; joint plans with the neighbours.
options.feedback: Correct. Fires in buildings under refurbishment spread through stripped compartmentation and accumulated waste — the plan attacks fuel, ignition and escape together, and includes the people next door.

options.text: Extinguishers and a fire point on every floor, a strict no-smoking rule enforced at the gate, hot work permits for the services cut-outs, and a weekly fire walk by the site manager to check exits and housekeeping.
options.feedback: Some of the right tools, but not a system for this building. The strip creates a growing fuel load and shrinking compartmentation — without daily waste removal, a temporary alarm and joint arrangements with the neighbours, a weekly walk finds the problems too late.

options.text: Treat fire as a standard-risk site: the frame is concrete and the floors non-combustible, so the company's generic fire procedure, extinguishers and the existing building alarm give proportionate cover for a strip-out.
options.feedback: The frame survives; the people don't. Strip waste, timber, packaging and temporary materials burn fiercely regardless of the frame, the existing alarm is being stripped out — and smoke doesn't respect party walls.
options.consequence: A waste fire in a stripped bay sent smoke through an opened riser into the neighbouring office; the office evacuated mid-morning and its landlord lodged a formal complaint with the client.

options.text: Each contractor manages fire for its own works under its own RAMS and hot work procedure, carrying its own extinguishers, with the principal contractor's role covering the induction fire briefing and the muster point.
options.feedback: Uncoordinated hot works above another trade's waste pile, attached to occupied premises, is how refurbishment fires start. Separate procedures leave no one controlling fuel, alarm and escape across the building — the PC owns the fire plan.
options.criticalFailure: No coordinated fire plan for a stripped building attached to occupied premises
options.consequence: A services contractor's hot cutting ignited another trade's waste on the fifth floor; with no fire watch or alarm it reached the roof void and the neighbouring offices were evacuated.

steps.topic: Fire risk in refurbishment
steps.learningNote: Refurbishment fire control: minimise and remove combustible waste daily, permit and fire-watch every hot work, keep a working alarm and lit escape routes as the building changes around them, retain compartmentation as long as possible, and plan jointly with attached occupied premises.

cppText.best: Fire plan: hot work permits with trained fire watch and 60-minute post-work checks; combustible strip waste cleared from floors daily, never stored in stairs, escape routes or the lane; temporary alarm maintained and tested weekly through the strip; escape routes and signage reviewed at every floor change; compartmentation retained as long as practicable; gas bottles in external locked cage; joint arrangements with neighbouring premises' responsible persons.
cppText.partial: Extinguishers and fire points provided; permit system and waste regime to be implemented before hot works.
cppText.poor: Fire arrangements generic — refurbishment-specific risks not addressed.
cppText.unsafe: No coordinated fire plan; hot works and waste uncontrolled.

phases.title: RAMS Review
phases.intro: Demolition and strip-out RAMS are where paper meets structure. If the method statement doesn't match the engineering and the sequence, reject it.

steps.prompt: The demolition contractor's RAMS for the rear annexe arrives. It is generic 'top-down demolition' text with no reference to the structural appraisal, no sequence drawings, no exclusion zone plan and nothing about the retained flank wall or the propping. The demolition start date is in ten days. Do you accept it?

options.text: Reject it with specific comments: require a written demolition plan built on the structural appraisal — sequence drawings, plant, exclusion zones, flank wall and propping interfaces, services isolation, and what to do if conditions differ.
options.feedback: Correct. Demolition must be planned in writing by competent people, and the plan must be engineered for this structure — a generic method statement cannot control a partial demolition against retained fabric.

options.text: Accept it as a provisional method so the start date holds, and send the contractor a conditions schedule requiring sequence drawings, exclusion zones and the flank wall and propping interface details before their machine arrives on site next week.
options.feedback: Closer — but conditions in an email don't reach the machine operator. The controlling document briefed to the gang must itself be right, and a 'provisional' acceptance tends to become the method.

options.text: Accept it: the firm is an established demolition specialist with trade-body membership and its own demolition engineers, and a top-down method is standard for a two-storey annexe of this size and construction.
options.feedback: Membership and in-house engineers are reassuring, but they haven't applied them to this RAMS. A 'standard' method doesn't control demolition against a retained flank wall and propping — review exists to prevent the collapse, not to explain it afterwards.
options.consequence: Working to the generic method, the gang pulled the annexe roof towards the retained wall; a section of parapet dropped inside the exclusion zone and demolition halted for a redesign.

options.text: Rewrite the RAMS yourself over the weekend using the structural appraisal and the TW drawings, then issue it to the demolition contractor on Monday so the start date holds and the method reflects this building.
options.feedback: The demolition contractor must own their method — and you are not the demolition engineer. A method statement the gang didn't write and their engineer didn't check controls nothing on the day.
options.consequence: The gang never adopted the rewritten method; their foreman worked to his own sequence and cut a slab edge before the retention steel was connected, triggering a stop and a re-plan.

steps.topic: Demolition planning — the written plan and its engineering basis
steps.learningNote: Before demolition: a structural appraisal by a competent person, a written demolition plan with sequence and methods, exclusion zones sized for the structure and plant, services isolated and proven dead, and defined arrangements for unexpected finds. The plan is engineering, not paperwork.

cppText.best: Demolition of rear annexe under a written demolition plan based on the structural appraisal: engineered top-down sequence, exclusion zones enforced, no personnel within the drop zone, flank wall retention and propping interfaces controlled at TWC hold points, services isolated and proven dead before work, daily condition review, defined stop-and-refer arrangements for unexpected conditions.
cppText.partial: Demolition RAMS accepted with conditions; sequence and interface detail to be completed before start.
cppText.poor: Generic demolition method statement accepted without engineering review.
cppText.unsafe: Demolition planned to proceed without an engineered written plan.

steps.prompt: The soft strip RAMS proposes stripping all six floors simultaneously to hit the programme, with the licensed asbestos removal 'working around' the strip gangs floor by floor. Your review?

options.text: Reject the sequencing. Strip follows asbestos removal area by area — no strip in any area until its four-stage clearance is complete — with escape routes and the temporary alarm maintained throughout, and waste removed from floors daily.
options.feedback: Correct. The sequence is survey, remove, clear, then strip. Strip gangs working alongside asbestos removal is how enclosures get breached and fibre spreads through a building full of people.

options.text: Accept the parallel working on condition that strip gangs keep at least one full floor between them and any live enclosure, with separate stair access and a daily coordination briefing between the two supervisors.
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but shared stairs, hoists and service risers still connect the floors — and the plan still depends on nobody making a mistake. Sequence the risk out instead: strip only behind clearance.

options.text: Accept it: the licensed contractor's enclosures are sealed, under negative pressure and smoke-tested daily, with air monitoring outside them, so other trades can work on the same floor beyond the barrier.
options.feedback: Enclosures control the removal area, not the building. Transit routes, waste bag runs and airlocks all interact with other trades — and the fewer people near live removal, the safer the work.
options.consequence: A strip operative's trolley tore an enclosure airlock on the third floor; air monitoring caught raised fibre levels, the floor was evacuated and decontaminated, and removal lost four days.

options.text: Accept it, and let strip gangs lift out ceiling grids in the visually cleaned bays of each enclosure floor while removal continues behind the polythene, so the analyst can clear each whole floor in one visit rather than returning bay by bay.
options.feedback: Unsafe. 'Visually cleaned' is not cleared. Mixed trades on a live removal floor puts unprotected workers a torn sheet away from licensed asbestos work.
options.criticalFailure: Strip-out permitted alongside live licensed asbestos removal
options.consequence: Ceiling grid lifted beside a live enclosure released residual debris; four strip operatives without RPE were exposed, and HSE served a prohibition notice and opened an investigation.

steps.topic: Strip-out sequencing with asbestos removal
steps.learningNote: In refurbishment the sequence protects people: asbestos removal completes and passes independent clearance area by area before strip enters. Programme is recovered by resource and logistics, never by overlapping trades with licensed asbestos work.

phases.title: Temporary Works Register
phases.intro: This project stands on its temporary works: the propping, the retained flank wall, the gantry over the public. Appoint the coordinator, build the register, and enforce the hold points.

steps.prompt: How is temporary works control set up for this project?

options.text: Appoint a trained Temporary Works Coordinator in writing with authority to stop work; keep a register of propping, flank wall retention, gantry, scaffold and the rest; design and check each item at the right category; and nothing loaded, struck or altered without the TWC's permit.
options.feedback: Correct. On a façade-retention-and-propping job the TWC's hold points are the difference between an engineered structure and a guess. The authority to stop work must be explicit.

options.text: Make the demolition contractor's engineer responsible for the propping and flank wall retention, since demolition loads them, with the scaffold supplier's designer covering the gantry and scaffold under their own register.
options.feedback: The propping, scaffold, gantry and demolition all interact — coordination must sit above the trades with the principal contractor's TWC, whoever designs the individual schemes. Two registers means nobody sees the interfaces.
options.consequence: With two registers, nobody checked how the demolition engineer's prop changes affected the scaffold supplier's loading bay; the slab under it deflected visibly and the bay was closed for a week.

options.text: Keep a temporary works list in the site diary, with each designer's drawings filed against their item, and review status, changes and any concerns with the trades and the scaffold contractor at the weekly coordination meeting.
options.feedback: A list without categories, checks and hold points is a memo, not control. Props get loaded, struck and altered between weekly meetings, and nobody holds the authority to say no.
options.consequence: The loading bay was stacked with plasterboard before its design check was signed off — no hold point existed to stop it; the platform deflected and had to be offloaded and re-checked.

options.text: Let the demolition foreman and machine operator decide on the day which props can come out as the annexe comes down, since they can see how the structure is behaving and no drawing anticipates every bay.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Props are removed to a designed, checked sequence under TWC control. Judging it from 'how the structure is behaving' is how progressive collapses start.
options.criticalFailure: Temporary works alterations left to operative judgement
options.consequence: The operator released two props he judged unloaded; a first-floor bay of the annexe dropped onto the slab below — a RIDDOR dangerous occurrence — and HSE served a prohibition notice.

steps.topic: Temporary works — coordination on a façade retention project
steps.learningNote: The TWC is appointed in writing, owns the register, ensures design and independent checking at the right category, and operates the hold points: permit to load, permit to strike, permission to alter. On retention schemes, monitoring results feed the TWC's decisions.

cppText.best: Temporary Works Coordinator appointed in writing with stop-work authority. Register covers propping to retained floors, flank wall retention, pavement gantry, sheeted scaffold, rubble chute, loading bay, pavement hoarding, plant back-propping and temporary services. Design and independent category checks per item; movement monitoring with trigger levels on retained structure; permits to load/strike at hold points; no alteration without TWC approval.
cppText.partial: TW register started; coordinator authority and hold points to be formalised before demolition.
cppText.poor: Temporary works managed trade-by-trade without central control.
cppText.unsafe: No temporary works control on a propping and retention project.

steps.prompt: Work through the temporary works items identified for this project. For each, decide the controls that apply.

items.name: Temporary propping to retained floors
items.description: Proprietary props and needles supporting retained floor plates through three storeys while structural openings are formed.
items.explanation: Multi-storey propping to a retained structure is engineered, independently checked by someone outside the design team, loaded and struck only at TWC hold points, and inspected against the design in place.

items.name: Flank wall retention scheme
items.description: Steel retention structure restraining the retained rear flank wall while the annexe is demolished against it.
items.explanation: Retention of a wall the public and workforce stand beside is the highest-consequence item on the register — bespoke design with the most rigorous level of independent check, movement monitoring with trigger levels, and hard hold points before demolition loads it.

items.name: Pavement gantry over the public footpath
items.description: Protective deck and support structure carrying the scaffold over the footpath, with the public walking beneath all day.
items.explanation: The gantry carries scaffold loads, stored materials and impact risk over the public — designed for its real loads including vehicle impact, independently checked, signed off before the footpath reopens beneath it, and inspected regularly and after any strike or storm.

items.name: Sheeted perimeter scaffold
items.description: Full-height independent scaffold with debris netting and sheeting, founded partly on the gantry.
items.explanation: Sheeting transforms the wind load case — this scaffold needs a bespoke design including the sheeted condition and its gantry support, handover before use, and inspection every 7 days and after alterations or weather.

items.name: Demolition exclusion zone hoarding and crash deck
items.description: Physical segregation and protective decking between the annexe demolition and the retained building's access routes.
items.explanation: Structures that protect people from demolition debris must resist the impacts the plan says they'll get — designed, checked, and verified in place before demolition starts behind them.

items.name: Rubble chute and scaffold support
items.description: Proprietary rubble chute fixed to the scaffold, discharging to a covered skip in the yard.
items.explanation: A proprietary chute is a standard solution, but it changes the scaffold's load case — the attachment is checked against the scaffold design, and the chute and its fixings are inspected in use.

items.name: Scaffold loading bay
items.description: Cantilevered loading platform at third-floor level for palletised materials via the lane-side hoist.
items.explanation: Loading bays carry concentrated loads and alter the scaffold design case — designed, checked, permit to load before first use, safe working load displayed.

items.name: Hoarding on the pavement licence line
items.description: Solid hoarding on the licensed pavement strip and the rear yard boundary, in the public's reach all day.
items.explanation: City-centre hoardings take wind funnelled between buildings and crowd loading — designed, checked and inspected periodically and after high winds.

items.name: Back-propping for plant on suspended slabs
items.description: Back-propping through two levels below where the mini excavator and skid-steer work on retained suspended floors.
items.explanation: A 1960s suspended slab was never designed for demolition plant — the loads are assessed, the back-propping designed and independently checked, and the machine does not track onto the slab until the TWC signs the hold point.

items.name: Temporary site services installation
items.description: Temporary electrics, lighting and distribution boards routed through the building during strip and refit.
items.explanation: Standard-solution temporary services still go on the register: installed to recognised standards by competent electricians, protected on escape routes, and inspected and tested on a schedule.

steps.topic: Temporary works register — retention, propping and public protection
steps.learningNote: On refurbishment, the register's high-consequence items are the ones holding up what you're keeping and protecting the people outside: retention schemes and multi-storey propping sit at the top categories with hard hold points; even proprietary kit registers and gets checked where it changes another structure's load case.

phases.title: Permits and Inspections
phases.intro: Permits gate the tasks that kill; inspections prove the props, scaffold and gantry are still doing what the design assumed.

steps.prompt: Select the permit systems this project genuinely needs. Over-permitting buries supervisors in paper; under-permitting leaves lethal tasks uncontrolled.

options.name: Demolition permit (daily authorisation to the plan)
Asbestos area clearance / re-entry certificate gate

steps.explanation: Hot works in a stripped building, daily demolition authorisation against the plan, loading and striking of propping and the gantry, a hard gate stopping any trade re-entering an asbestos area without its independent clearance certificate, isolation and proving-dead of the building's services, and the crane lifts placing the gantry and retention steels over the footpath all need permit control. There is no ground-breaking in this scope, and no confined space entry — those permits would be paperwork without purpose.
steps.topic: Permit to work systems for refurbishment and demolition
steps.learningNote: A permit is a formal, time-bounded check that controls are in place immediately before a high-risk task, with sign-back at the end. On refurbishment, treat asbestos clearance certificates as a permit gate: no certificate, no re-entry — no exceptions for 'a quick look'.

steps.prompt: Set the inspection and monitoring regime for the project.

options.text: Scaffold inspected before use, every 7 days and after alteration or bad weather; gantry checked after storms or impacts; retained wall and props monitored against trigger levels; lifting certificates checked; daily supervisor checks and a weekly recorded manager's inspection.
options.feedback: Correct. Statutory inspections are the floor. On a retention job the monitoring regime with defined trigger levels — and who acts when they're hit — is what turns instruments into control.

options.text: Each specialist inspects and records its own works at the statutory frequencies — the scaffolder the scaffold and gantry, the demolition engineer the retained wall, the asbestos supervisor the enclosures — with copies sent to you weekly.
options.feedback: They do inspect their own works — but the interfaces (demolition vibration on the retained wall, chute loads on the scaffold, waste against escape routes) and the response to trigger levels belong to the principal contractor's regime, not a weekly copy file.

options.text: Rely on the visiting safety advisor's monthly audit, which samples scaffold tags, TW records and monitoring data, with the scaffold contractor's weekly tag inspection covering the statutory scaffold requirement between visits.
options.feedback: Monthly sampling is far outside the frequency a moving demolition face and a monitored retained wall need. Audits check the system; they are not the system — and nobody here acts on the monitoring triggers or checks the gantry after weather.
options.consequence: Readings on the flank wall crept towards the amber trigger for a fortnight with nobody reviewing them; the trend surfaced at the monthly audit and demolition halted for redesign.

options.text: Inspect by exception: the gangs report defects to their supervisors, the scaffolder attends when called, and the monitoring targets on the retained wall are read whenever a crack or movement is spotted.
options.feedback: Retained walls don't show distress until they move, and defects rarely get reported by the people who caused them. Reactive inspection on a retention project is waiting for the crack.
options.criticalFailure: No planned inspection or monitoring regime
options.consequence: Unread, movement in the retained flank wall went unnoticed until brickwork fell into the yard — a RIDDOR dangerous occurrence — and the lane was closed while HSE investigated.

steps.topic: Inspections and structural monitoring
steps.learningNote: Statutory rhythm plus engineering rhythm: scaffold 7-day/after events; gantry and hoarding after storms and strikes; movement monitoring on retained structure at designed frequency with trigger levels and a named response; thorough examinations checked at the gate; daily and weekly management layers on top.

cppText.best: Inspection schedule: scaffold before first use, every 7 days and after alteration/adverse weather; gantry and pavement hoarding checked after storms and any impact; movement monitoring on retained flank wall and propping at designed frequency with trigger levels and named escalation; lifting equipment thorough-examination certificates verified on arrival; daily supervisor pre-start checks; weekly recorded manager's inspection; actions tracked to closure.
cppText.partial: Statutory inspections planned; monitoring trigger levels and escalation to be confirmed.
cppText.poor: Inspection left to individual trades without PC oversight.
cppText.unsafe: No planned inspection or monitoring regime.

phases.title: High-Risk Activities
phases.intro: The annexe comes down and the asbestos comes out. These are the weeks where the planning is tested for real.

steps.prompt: Sequence the annexe works safely: from asbestos removal through retention and back-propping to machine demolition against the retained flank wall.
steps.context: The flank wall retention is a category 3 scheme; back-propping for plant on the retained slabs is category 2. The neighbours, the lane and the public footpath stay live throughout.

activities.label: Design check certificates for retention and back-props
activities.detail: Independent cat 3 check for the flank wall retention, cat 2 for back-propping, logged by the TWC.

activities.label: Licensed asbestos removal in annexe and interface bays
activities.detail: Notified in advance, under enclosure with negative pressure and airlocks.

activities.label: Four-stage clearance and reoccupation certificate
activities.detail: Independent analyst: preliminary check, visual inspection, air test, final assessment.

activities.label: Soft strip and salvage; services isolated and proven dead
activities.detail: All salvage complete and every service to the annexe cut back and confirmed dead.

activities.label: Install flank wall retention steel and back-props
activities.detail: Erected to the checked drawings by the TW contractor; fixings drilled into the cleared fabric.

activities.label: TWC inspects the installed works; permit to load
activities.detail: Hold point: the retention and back-props accepted as built before any load is put on them.

activities.label: Demolition permit issued; exclusion zone set and swept
activities.detail: Daily authorisation to the written plan; zone set by structure, plant reach and debris throw.

activities.label: Top-down machine demolition to the engineered sequence
activities.detail: Monitoring read to schedule; stop and refer to the designer on any unexpected movement.

constraints.reason: Clearance can only certify an area once licensed removal in it is complete.
Strip gangs entering before the reoccupation certificate are exposed to residual asbestos fibre.
Temporary works are erected only to a design that has passed its independent check.
Fixing retention steel drills and cuts into interface fabric that must be cleared of asbestos first.
The TWC can only accept and permit what has actually been installed and inspected.
The demolition permit depends on the retention and back-props having passed their hold point.
No demolition permit while services are live or salvage gangs are still working inside the annexe.
Machine demolition without the permit and a swept exclusion zone puts people in the drop zone.
Taking out annexe structure before the retention is accepted can bring the flank wall down onto the yard and lane.

steps.topic: Demolition and retention — BS 5975 hold points, BS 6187 planning, CAR 2012 clearance
steps.learningNote: Remove the asbestos, prove it clear, strip and isolate, then install and accept the temporary works — and only then authorise the machine. The retention scheme's permit to load is the gate: no structure that the flank wall relies on comes out until the TWC has accepted the scheme as built.

steps.prompt: Annexe demolition begins Monday. The demolition foreman proposes keeping two operatives inside the annexe cutting out services and salvage while the excavator processes the far end — 'they'll stay a bay apart'. Your decision?

options.text: No. Hold to the demolition plan: strip and salvage done before the machine starts, nobody in the exclusion zone while it works, the designed top-down sequence, TWC hold points at the props and retained wall, and stop-and-refer on anything unexpected.
options.feedback: Correct. People and demolition machines don't share a structure. 'A bay apart' assumes the building fails politely — partial collapse doesn't respect bay lines.

options.text: Allow it for this shift only, with a dedicated banksman watching the structure, radios for the two operatives, an agreed horn signal to clear out, and the excavator working from the far end back towards them.
options.feedback: By the time a banksman sees movement, the collapse has started — progressive failure in a 1960s structure gives seconds, not minutes, and a machine working back towards them closes the gap every hour.
options.consequence: Debris from a slab the machine was processing fell through two bays and landed near the operatives cutting services; nobody was hurt, but demolition stopped for an investigation.

options.text: Allow it: the foreman has demolished larger frames than this, the operatives hold demolition cards, and the bays are separated by a full-height wall, so a two-bay buffer gives a reasonable margin.
options.feedback: Experience, cards and an internal wall don't change structural behaviour. The exclusion zone exists because nobody can predict exactly how a cut structure lets go — and internal walls are often what is being cut.
options.consequence: The full-height wall the foreman relied on came down with the adjacent bay; masonry fell into the operatives' bay seconds after they had moved, and demolition halted for an investigation.

options.text: Allow it, and keep the strip gang working in the retained building's ground-floor bays next to the annexe as well, since they are behind the party wall, outside the machine's reach on the plan and clear of the drop zone.
options.feedback: Unsafe twice over: workers inside the demolition structure, and workers against the very wall the demolition is loading. The exclusion zone includes the adjacent bays because the plan says it does.
options.criticalFailure: Personnel permitted inside the demolition exclusion zone during machine demolition
options.consequence: An annexe beam was dragged through the party wall into the ground-floor bay; a strip operative suffered a fractured shoulder, a RIDDOR-reportable injury, and HSE served a prohibition notice.

steps.topic: Demolition — exclusion zones and structural instability
steps.learningNote: Machine demolition and people never mix inside the exclusion zone, and the zone is set by the engineering — structure, plant reach and debris throw — not by convenience. Strip and salvage finish before the machine starts, and unexpected structural behaviour means stop and refer to the engineer.

steps.prompt: The licensed contractor is removing asbestos insulation board ceilings on floors two and three. The fit-out contractor asks to send surveyors into floor two 'as soon as the enclosure comes down' to hold the programme. What governs re-entry?

options.text: The four-stage clearance: no one re-enters until the independent analyst has completed the visual inspection and air test and issued the certificate of reoccupation — the site rules make that certificate the re-entry permit.
options.feedback: Correct. The enclosure comes down after clearance, not before, and the analyst's certificate — independent of the removal contractor — is the only key that reopens the area.

options.text: The licensed removal supervisor's written sign-off that the area is clean and visually inspected, with the analyst's certificate following within the week — the supervisor ran the enclosure and knows it best.
options.feedback: The removal contractor cannot clear their own work — that independence is the whole point of the four-stage clearance. Until the analyst certifies, the area is still a controlled asbestos area.
options.consequence: Surveyors entered on the supervisor's sign-off; the analyst's later visual inspection found debris behind a riser panel, and the floor was re-sealed and re-cleaned, losing a week.

options.text: Allow the fit-out surveyors in once the enclosure is down and the air test is under way, provided they wear FFP3 masks and disposable coveralls, keep out of the removal bays, and are logged in and out by the asbestos supervisor.
options.feedback: RPE is not a substitute for clearance, and the enclosure should not be down before clearance anyway. Uncleared areas remain controlled asbestos areas — masks don't change who is allowed in.
options.consequence: The surveyors walked through during the air test, which then failed; they had to be decontaminated, the clearance restarted and fit-out surveying lost another week.

options.text: Bring the floor-two enclosure down tonight so both trades gain a day: the removal is finished, the air test can be done on the open floor tomorrow, and any residue will come up in the builder's clean.
options.feedback: Unsafe and unlawful. Striking an enclosure before the visual inspection and clearance releases any residual fibre into a building full of workers — and 'the builder's clean' spreads it further.
options.criticalFailure: Asbestos enclosure removal before four-stage clearance
options.consequence: Air tests after the early strike failed; residual fibre had spread to floor three, two trades were exposed, and HSE served a prohibition notice halting work on both floors.

steps.topic: Licensed asbestos removal — clearance and re-entry
steps.learningNote: Licensed work runs: notification to the regulator in advance, enclosure under negative pressure with airlocks, controlled removal, then the independent analyst's four-stage clearance — preliminary check, visual, air test, final assessment — before the certificate of reoccupation opens the area. The certificate is the permit; nothing else is.

phases.title: Environmental Management
phases.intro: Thousands of tonnes of waste, and neighbours a party wall away — the environmental controls on this job are as visible as the scaffolding.

steps.prompt: The strip and demolition will produce mixed strip-out waste, concrete and brick, plus hazardous streams: asbestos, fluorescent tubes, old refrigerant units and contaminated materials. Set the waste management arrangements.
