options.text: Segregate at source, hazardous streams kept apart; check each carrier's registration and receiving site's permit; transfer notes for every load, consignment notes for hazardous waste; asbestos in a locked, labelled skip via the licensed contractor; track against the waste plan.
options.feedback: Correct. The duty of care follows your waste to its final destination — segregation, documented transfers and verified carriers are what stands between you and someone else's fly-tip carrying your paperwork.

options.text: Send mixed strip waste to a permitted transfer station that sorts it, with transfer notes for every load, the asbestos handled by the licensed contractor, and the tubes and refrigerant units flagged to the driver for separate handling.
options.feedback: Mixed general waste can lawfully go for sorting — but hazardous streams like tubes and refrigerant units must be separated and travel under consignment notes. Flagging them to a driver is not a consignment note.

options.text: Let each subcontractor remove its own waste under its own carrier and paperwork, since they price for it and know their streams, and collect copies of their transfer notes at the monthly progress meeting.
options.feedback: Fragmented waste arrangements on a demolition job mean no one can evidence the duty of care day to day — the yard fills with unclaimed piles and the monthly copies arrive incomplete.
options.consequence: Fly-tipped plasterboard carrying the project's labels was found in a lay-by; no trade could produce a transfer note for it, and the council opened a duty-of-care investigation.

options.text: Double-bag the fluorescent tubes and small hazardous items and place them in the general skip, labelled, so the transfer station can pull them out at sorting — they are a few bags in a large mixed load.
options.feedback: Hazardous waste in the general stream is an offence, bagged and labelled or not — and mercury from tubes crushed in the skip contaminates the whole load.
options.criticalFailure: Hazardous waste concealed in the general waste stream
options.consequence: The transfer station rejected the load after finding crushed tubes; the Environment Agency investigated the mis-described waste and the whole skip had to be disposed of as hazardous.

steps.topic: Waste duty of care and hazardous waste
steps.learningNote: Duty of care: describe your waste accurately, keep hazardous streams separate with consignment notes, use registered carriers and permitted sites, and keep the paperwork. On demolition jobs, check destinations — cheap disposal usually means someone else's field.

cppText.best: Environmental controls: waste segregated at source; hazardous streams (asbestos, tubes, refrigerants, contaminated material) separately contained with consignment notes; carriers' registrations and receiving sites' permits verified; transfer notes retained; asbestos in locked labelled skip via licensed contractor; dust suppression at source; noisy works within hours agreed with the local authority; noise and vibration monitoring with trigger levels; drain protection in the lane; complaints log with named responder.
cppText.partial: Waste segregation established; hazardous documentation and monitoring arrangements to be completed.
cppText.poor: Waste and nuisance controls left to individual contractors.
cppText.unsafe: Hazardous waste entering the general stream — non-compliant.

steps.prompt: Demolition and slab-breaking will be the noisiest, dustiest weeks of the project, with offices working next door and shoppers under the gantry. What do you put in place?

options.text: Agree noise consent and hours with the local authority before demolition; best practicable means — crushing rather than impact breaking where possible, screens, idle plant off; monitor noise and vibration at the party walls; damp dust at source; tell the neighbours ahead.
options.feedback: Correct. Agreeing consented hours and methods with the authority in advance protects the programme as much as the neighbours — it converts complaint risk into an agreed envelope you can plan within.

options.text: Work standard site hours, keep plant serviced and fitted with silencers, damp down during breaking, and deal promptly with any complaint the council or the neighbours raise, adjusting methods if a pattern emerges.
options.feedback: Good housekeeping, but reactive nuisance management on a city-centre demolition invites an abatement notice — which stops the noisy works on the council's timetable, not yours. Agree the envelope in advance.

options.text: Programme the slab breaking for nights and weekends, when the offices are empty and the shops are shut, so the worst of the noise falls when nobody is next door and the daytime programme stays quiet for the neighbours.
options.feedback: City centres have residents, hotels and licensing hours too — night working needs its own consent, usually creates a worse nuisance problem than it solves, and adds fatigue and lone working to the riskiest weeks.
options.consequence: Residents in the flats above the shops complained on the first night of breaking; the council served a notice restricting the works and slab-breaking slipped while consent was renegotiated.

options.text: Start the breakers at 7am and finish the heaviest breaking by 9:30, before the offices fill up, then switch the gang to quieter tasks, so the worst noise lands when the fewest people are at their desks next door.
options.feedback: Starting noisy works early without agreed hours is exactly what triggers formal action, however reasonable the logic — and the client's name is on the hoarding the complaints mention.
options.consequence: The office next door complained to the council about the 7am starts; environmental health imposed restricted hours on all noisy works, adding two weeks to the slab-breaking.

steps.topic: Noise, vibration and dust in the city centre
steps.learningNote: Engage the local authority early and agree hours, methods and limits before the noisy phase — described generically, a noise consent for the works. Then deliver best practicable means: quieter methods first, screens, maintenance, monitoring with trigger levels, water on the dust at source, and neighbours told before it starts.

phases.title: Incident / Challenge Events
phases.intro: The building, the weather and the city will all test your plan. Your judgement under pressure is what's being assessed.

steps.prompt: EVENT: Mid-morning during annexe demolition, the machine operator stops and points out a fresh diagonal crack in the retained flank wall, above the retention steelwork. The monitoring isn't due to be read until tomorrow.

options.text: Stop demolition at once, clear and extend the exclusion zone — closing the lane or footpath with the authority if needed — take a monitoring reading now, and have the TWC and retention designer assess before any restart.
options.feedback: Correct. A new crack in retained structure during demolition is a stop-work trigger. The engineer decides what it means; your job is to get people out of the consequence zone and the data to the designer fast.

options.text: Fix dated tell-tales across the crack ends, photograph it, email the TWC and carry on at reduced pace, reviewing the position at tomorrow's scheduled monitoring read.
options.feedback: Tell-tales and photographs are useful records, but they measure movement over days. A wall being actively loaded by demolition can fail before tomorrow's read — the work loading it must stop first.
options.consequence: The crack widened through the afternoon and brickwork dropped from the parapet into the yard; nobody was hit, but demolition was suspended for a week of remedial retention.

options.text: Move the machine to the far end of the annexe, keep the rear lane cordoned off, and ask the TWC to come and look at it this afternoon, while demolition continues on the bays that don't bear on the retained wall or its steelwork.
options.feedback: Relocating the work helps, but continuing any demolition on a structure showing unexplained distress, before the designer has assessed it, is still guessing at structural behaviour — and no reading has been taken.

options.text: Record the crack in the diary with dated photographs and carry on to programme — fine cracking is common in 1960s brickwork under vibration, and tomorrow's scheduled read will show whether anything has really moved.
options.feedback: Unsafe. A fresh diagonal crack above retention steel during demolition is the wall telling you the load path has changed. Carrying on risks a collapse onto the site and possibly the lane.
options.criticalFailure: Demolition continued after unexplained cracking in retained structure
options.consequence: The crack opened overnight and part of the retained flank wall collapsed into the yard — a RIDDOR dangerous occurrence; HSE served a prohibition notice on all demolition.

steps.topic: Structural distress during demolition
steps.learningNote: Unexpected cracking or movement in retained structure is an automatic stop: clear the consequence zone (which may include public areas), get an immediate monitoring read, and restart only on the temporary works designer's assessment. Programme never overrules a structure behaving off-plan.

steps.prompt: EVENT: An HSE inspector arrives unannounced at the gate mid-strip, saying they're visiting refurbishment sites in the area and want to look at your asbestos controls and the gantry.

options.text: Check their ID, take them through induction and accompany them; provide what they ask for — F10, CPP, asbestos survey, notifications and clearance certificates, TW register and gantry records — answer honestly and act promptly on what they raise.
options.feedback: Correct. Inspectors have a right of entry, and a well-run site treats a visit as a free audit. Openness plus prompt action is also how you avoid a follow-up visit becoming enforcement.

options.text: Check their warrant, sit them in the site office with the document folders and a coffee, and ask the supervisors to spend half an hour tidying the strip floors and clearing the gantry deck before the walk-round starts, so the visit runs smoothly.
options.feedback: Delaying an inspector so the floors can be tidied reads as concealment — and they have seen the tidy-up sprint before. The site's normal state is what is being inspected.
options.consequence: From the office window the inspector watched waste being cleared off the gantry; she widened the visit, found the load notice exceeded and issued a material breach letter with fee for intervention.

options.text: Confirm their identity, then ask them to wait at the gate until the company's safety director is on the phone and head office has confirmed the visit, as the company's enforcement procedure requires.
options.feedback: Verify identification, certainly — but inspectors don't need an appointment or head office's permission, and keeping them at the gate looks like obstruction, which is an offence in itself.
options.consequence: The inspector recorded the delay at the gate, then inspected in full and widened the visit; the hostile start ended with a fee-for-intervention invoice for the breaches found.

options.text: Take them in, but radio the floors first to pause the dry cutting and keep the strip gangs on the upper floors away from the walk-round route until the inspector has seen the gantry and left.
options.feedback: Concealing work activity from an inspector is deception. If discovered — and it usually is — it converts advice into enforcement and destroys your credibility for the rest of the project.
options.criticalFailure: Attempted to conceal site conditions from an HSE inspector
options.consequence: The inspector heard cutting restart upstairs, went up and found dry cutting with no RPE; she served a prohibition notice and recorded the attempt to keep the work from view.

steps.topic: Regulator visits — rights of entry and response
steps.learningNote: Inspectors may enter at any reasonable time, examine, question and require documents. Verify identity, accompany, be straight, and treat findings as free consultancy: act, record the action, and reply. Enforcement follows concealment far more often than it follows honesty.

phases.title: Progress Review
phases.intro: Mid-project: demolition is done, the refit is ramping up, and the client, the programme and the neighbours all want something from you.

steps.prompt: The asbestos removal overran and the project is three weeks behind. The client's asset manager wants the lost time recovered before the pre-let fit-out date and suggests 'running the remaining strip, first fix and the external recladding all in parallel, seven days a week'. Your response?

options.text: Re-plan: find what genuinely compresses — procurement, hoist logistics, extra supervised gangs in separated areas — assess fire, escape and trade-stacking risks before agreeing, and offer a recovery programme you can supervise.
options.feedback: Correct. Recovery comes from logistics and resource, engineered floor by floor — not from stacking trades in a part-stripped building until the fire plan and supervision can't cover them.

options.text: Agree to the seven-day parallel working for six weeks: the trades want the overtime, supervision can be covered on a rota, and the fire plan already allows hot works on any floor under permit.
options.feedback: Uncontrolled trade-stacking plus fatigue in a part-stripped building with live hot works and changing escape routes is how refurbishment fires and falls happen. A supervision rota and a permit system don't stretch to cover it.
options.consequence: Three trades stacked on one floor at the weekend left hot works beside fresh strip waste; a smouldering pile was found at the end-of-shift check and the parallel working was halted for a re-plan.

options.text: Write to the client setting out that the overrun arose from asbestos quantities beyond the survey, that it is a compensation event under the contract, and that the completion date must move by three weeks rather than be recovered at risk.
options.feedback: The contractual position may well be sound, but a letter isn't a recovery plan. There are usually safe weeks to be found in logistics and sequencing — refusing to look costs the relationship and possibly the next contract.
options.consequence: The asset manager escalated to the client's board, the pre-let tenant threatened to withdraw, and the client held back the next phase of work while the dispute ran on.

options.text: Recover time by moving to a single whole-building clearance at the end of removal instead of area by area, letting strip and fit-out follow the removal gangs as each floor is visually complete.
options.feedback: The area-by-area clearance gate is the control, not a bottleneck. Letting trades follow on a visual 'looks complete' exposes every following trade to whatever the analyst would have found.
options.criticalFailure: Proposed bypassing asbestos clearance certificates under programme pressure
options.consequence: Joiners worked behind the removal gangs on floor four; the final clearance found residual debris there, the trades had been exposed, and HSE served a prohibition notice.

steps.topic: Programme recovery without de-controlling
steps.learningNote: Recover programme by re-sequencing, resourcing and logistics — never by removing gates. Trade-stacking in refurbishment multiplies fire load, blocks escape routes and outruns supervision; model those risks before you promise the client anything.

steps.prompt: The complaints log shows a pattern: the shop complains about deliveries at their busiest hour, the office about noise during conference calls, and both say 'nobody tells us anything'. How do you manage the neighbours for the second half?

options.text: Get ahead of it: a named contact on the hoarding, a fortnightly look-ahead to both neighbours flagging disruptive works, deliveries moved off the shop's peak, monthly liaison, and every complaint logged, answered and closed out.
options.feedback: Correct. Neighbour management is risk management: informed neighbours tolerate more, complain less, and phone you instead of the council. On a 34-week city job, that goodwill is programme insurance.

options.text: Have the site manager call each complainant back the same day with an apology and an explanation, give the office manager a direct number for quiet-hours requests, and send both neighbours a goodwill hamper at the project's halfway point.
options.feedback: Courtesy helps, but it's reactive — the pattern in the log is a planning failure (deliveries and noise landing at the worst times), and only planning ahead and telling the neighbours in advance fixes it.

options.text: Route all neighbour contact through the client's managing agent, who holds the leases and the relationships, and supply them with a monthly works summary to pass on to the shop and office tenants.
options.feedback: The principal contractor controls the site causing the disturbance. Passing neighbours through the landlord's agent slows every answer, multiplies the frustration and lands back on you with the client's anger attached.
options.consequence: Complaints routed through the agent took a week to reach site; the office went to the council instead, and environmental health imposed conditions on the noisy works.

options.text: Keep logging the complaints but hold the current arrangements: disruption is unavoidable on a demolition job, the works are lawful and within agreed hours, and moving delivery slots now would cost programme.
options.feedback: Unanswered complainants escalate to the council, and a statutory nuisance notice will set your working hours for you. 'Lawful' is not the same as acceptable to the people next door.
options.consequence: The shop's owner went to the council and the local press; a nuisance investigation followed, and the client's asset manager demanded a weekly neighbour report.

steps.topic: Neighbour and stakeholder management
steps.learningNote: Treat neighbours as an interface to manage, not noise to endure: a named contact, advance notice of disruptive works, logistics planned around their business, and a complaints loop that visibly changes something. It is cheaper than one abatement notice.

cppText.best: Communication: induction before entry; daily activity briefings and pre-task RAMS briefings; weekly coordination meeting across strip, demolition, asbestos and TW trades; named neighbour contact displayed on hoarding; fortnightly neighbour look-ahead note and monthly liaison meeting; complaints logged, answered and closed with actions; F10, insurance and site rules displayed.
cppText.partial: Internal communication established; neighbour liaison to be formalised.
cppText.poor: Communication reactive; neighbours informed only after complaints.

phases.title: Handover
phases.intro: A refurbished building's most valuable handover document is an honest record of what's still in it — finish the information as carefully as the finishes.

steps.prompt: Practical completion is three weeks away. What does a proper handover require on this project?

options.text: Give the principal designer the H&S file information — an updated asbestos register of every ACM removed and retained, clearance and consignment records, as-builts of the altered structure, residual risks, O&Ms — and plan the gantry and scaffold strike as temporary works.
options.feedback: Correct. The updated asbestos register and the structural record are what protect the next twenty years of maintenance and refurbishment in this building — and demobilising the gantry over a live footpath is a temporary works operation, not a tidy-up.

options.text: Hand over at practical completion with the O&Ms and the commissioning certificates, and let the H&S file and asbestos records follow over the next couple of months as subcontractors submit their close-out packs.
options.feedback: Information chased after the teams have demobilised is incomplete information — and an incomplete asbestos register is a trap for the client's next contractor.
options.consequence: The asbestos close-out pack never arrived; the tenant's fit-out contractor drilled into a riser with retained ACMs on a register nobody held, and the work was stopped for sampling.

options.text: Reference the removal contractor's records in the file and leave the originals with them — licensed contractors keep their job records for years, so the client or a future contractor can request them if they are ever needed.
options.feedback: The client's duty to manage asbestos in the building depends on an updated register being in their hands at handover, including what was retained. 'Available on request' is how records get lost — and firms close.
options.consequence: At handover the client's facilities manager asked for the updated asbestos register and nobody could produce it; practical completion was withheld until the records were retrieved.

options.text: Concentrate the last three weeks on the snagging the incoming tenant will see, and assemble the H&S file from the project server after completion, when the site team has time to do it thoroughly.
options.feedback: Cosmetics over content. The residual risk information — what is still in the ceilings and risers, what the props did to the structure — is what prevents the next refurbishment's exposure incident, and it is gathered before the team leaves.
options.consequence: The file was compiled late from incomplete server records; the as-builts omitted the new slab openings and trimming, and the tenant's fit-out design had to be redone.

steps.topic: Handover — H&S file, asbestos register and demobilisation
steps.learningNote: On refurbishment the file must tell the truth about the building: ACMs removed and retained (with certificates), structural alterations, residual risks and maintenance access. Demobilisation — gantry strike, scaffold strike, hoarding removal, footpath reinstatement — is planned and TW-controlled like everything else.

cppText.best: Handover: H&S file information to Principal Designer including updated asbestos register (ACMs removed with clearance certificates; ACMs retained with locations), structural as-builts and propping records, residual risks and safe maintenance access; O&Ms and commissioning certificates complete; waste documentation archived; gantry and scaffold strike planned under TW control with authority liaison for footpath reinstatement; client familiarisation completed.
cppText.partial: Handover information partially assembled at completion.
cppText.poor: Handover records left to follow after completion.
cppText.unsafe: No structured handover of asbestos and structural information.

phases.title: Final Score and Feedback
phases.intro: Project complete. Review your performance across every discipline.

steps.title: Building handed back
body: The scaffold and gantry are down, the footpath is reinstated, and the client has taken the refurbished building back with a complete record of what was removed and what remains.

Your decisions across 34 weeks of surveys, strip-out, demolition, temporary works, asbestos control and neighbour management have been assessed across legal compliance, safety control, planning, temporary works, environment, programme and quality.
Continue to your score report, Construction Phase Plan, registers and trackers — and see how your site set-up compared with the model answer.
keyPoints: Review your missed items report — those are your revision topics
Download your CPP, registers and trackers for tutor discussion
Try the scenario again and beat your grade

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: A strip operative on the fourth floor — an area the survey listed as clear — pulls down a ceiling tile and finds broken board debris and old pipe lagging remnants in the void above.

options.text: Stop work in the area at once, get everyone out, seal and sign it, keep clothing and tools inside, have an accredited surveyor sample it, and review whether the survey can be relied on in similar voids elsewhere.
options.feedback: Correct. Stop, seal, sample. And a find in one 'clear' void puts every similar void in doubt — the survey's reliability is now a live question across the building.

options.text: Move the gang to the floor below, tape off the ceiling bay, and have the asbestos contractor's supervisor look at the debris and take a sample when they are next on site on Thursday.
options.feedback: Relocating the gang is right, but the area needs sealing and signing now, the find reporting today, and sampling arranged urgently — not when a visit happens to be scheduled.

options.text: Stop the gang, photograph the debris and the lagging, and email the images to the surveyor who carried out the R&D survey for an identification before deciding whether the licensed contractor needs to be brought back in.
options.feedback: Stopping is right, but nobody can identify asbestos from a photograph. While the email thread grows, the void is open, the area unsealed and the find unreported.
options.consequence: While the photographs were discussed, another trade walked through the unsealed area and tracked debris along the corridor; two floors needed specialist cleaning and clearance.

options.text: Have the operative, who holds asbestos awareness training, damp down and double-bag the debris in a red bag for the licensed contractor, then carry on taking down the ceiling grid across the rest of the floor.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Awareness training teaches recognition and avoidance, not handling — and continuing to pull ceilings under a contaminated void spreads fibre across the floor.
options.criticalFailure: Strip continued after discovery of suspect asbestos materials
options.consequence: Sampling later confirmed amosite in the debris; the operative and his gang had been exposed while pulling the grid, and HSE served a prohibition notice on the strip.

eventPool.learningNote: The drill never changes: stop, get people out, seal and sign, don't disturb further, sample by competent people, and reassess the survey's reliability everywhere similar. Surveys have limits — voids, risers and ducts produce surprises, and the response is what protects people.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: Overnight storm winds have torn a large section of the scaffold sheeting at fifth-floor level. At 7am it is flapping loose over the gantry and the footpath below, and shops open at 9.

options.text: Cordon the footpath below with the authority as needed; have the scaffold contractor's CISRS-carded scaffolders re-secure or remove the sheeting from safe positions; and require a recorded inspection, ties included, before reuse.
options.feedback: Correct. Torn sheeting means the scaffold took loads outside its normal case and now has debris risk over the public. Exclusion first, competent hands aloft, and an after-weather inspection before anyone works from it.

options.text: Send two of the site labourers up the internal ladder access with harnesses and cable ties to secure the flapping section from the fifth lift before the shops open, then book the scaffold contractor in to look at the fixings later in the week.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Untrained operatives improvising on a wind-damaged scaffold at fifth-floor level is a fall and a dropped-object risk in one — harnesses don't make it a planned task, and cable ties don't restore a designed sheeting fixing.
options.criticalFailure: Untrained operatives sent to repair storm-damaged scaffold at height
options.consequence: A labourer slipped on a displaced board at the fifth lift and was left suspended in his harness with a shoulder injury; HSE investigated the RIDDOR report.

options.text: Leave the sheeting until the scaffold contractor's routine visit on Thursday — the gantry fan and deck are designed to catch falling debris, and the forecast shows the wind easing through the day.
options.feedback: The gantry protects against falling material, not against a sail of sheeting and fittings coming off the fifth lift in the next gust — and the scaffold's own condition after the storm is unverified.
options.consequence: A gust that afternoon tore the sheeting free with two fittings attached; it landed across the footpath beyond the gantry, narrowly missing shoppers, and the pavement was closed.

options.text: Cordon the footpath below, then have the scaffolders strip the sheeting off the whole front elevation so the wind can't catch it again, and re-sheet once the stormy spell has passed.
options.feedback: Cordoning is right, but wholesale unsheeting swaps one problem for dust and debris migration over the neighbours — repair to the design, and check why the fixing detail failed.

eventPool.topic: Scaffold sheeting and wind — after-weather response
eventPool.learningNote: Sheeting turns a scaffold into a sail — the design allows for it, but storms demand response: exclude below, competent scaffolders only, and a recorded inspection after adverse weather before reuse. Repair to the design detail, not with whatever's in the van.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: On your morning walk you find twenty bags of strip-out waste stacked in the rear lane against the neighbouring office's fire exit door, left by the night-shift clearance gang for today's collection.

options.text: Clear the exit now, before anything else; then tell the neighbour, find out why the gang staged waste there, change the waste flow so the lane is never a holding area, and brief every shift on the neighbours' escape routes.
options.feedback: Correct. A blocked fire exit is cleared now, personally if necessary. Then fix the system: the night gang staged waste there because the plan gave them nowhere better — that's yours to solve.

options.text: Radio the waste contractor to bring today's lane collection forward to first thing, post a labourer by the bags to keep the door area watched, and raise the staging location with the night-shift supervisor.
options.feedback: First thing is still hours of a blocked escape route for a building full of office workers — a labourer watching the bags doesn't clear the door. If they evacuate at 9:15, the bags are still there.
options.consequence: The office ran a fire drill at 9:15; staff pushing the exit door met the waste bags and had to turn back, and the neighbour's landlord made a formal complaint to the client.

options.text: Clear the exit straight away with the yard labourers, move the waste into the yard skip, and tell the night supervisor never to stage waste in the lane again — no harm came of it, so there is no reason to worry the neighbour about it.
options.feedback: The immediate risk is fixed, but hiding it wastes the trust-building opportunity and leaves their fire warden ignorant of a risk they should be watching for too.

options.text: Leave the bags for the booked Friday collection: the office has two other exits, that door is rarely used, and carrying them back through the building would put loose waste back on the strip floors.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Fire exits exist for the five minutes nobody predicts. Blocking a neighbour's escape route with combustible waste for days is indefensible in every sense.
options.criticalFailure: Neighbouring premises' fire exit left blocked by site waste
options.consequence: The bags were set alight overnight; the fire scorched the office's exit door, the neighbouring building closed for a day, and a formal fire safety investigation followed.

eventPool.topic: Fire escape routes and site waste logistics
eventPool.learningNote: Escape routes — yours and your neighbours' — are never storage, not for an hour. When you find one blocked, clear it before investigating; then fix the logistics that put waste there, because rules without a workable waste flow will be broken again tonight.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: The office manager next door calls at 7:20am: your breakers have been running since 7:00, but the hours agreed with the local authority for noisy works start at 8:00. The slab-breaking gang say they were told to 'get ahead' by their supervisor.

options.text: Stop the noisy works until 8:00, call the office manager back personally with an apology and what you've done, find out how the agreed hours were overridden, re-brief the gangs on the consent conditions, and log the complaint.
options.feedback: Correct. The agreed hours are a condition you operate under, not a guideline. Stop, respond personally, fix the instruction chain that broke — and show the neighbour the system working.

options.text: Call the office manager back to apologise and explain, let the gang finish the bay they've started — stopping mid-bay leaves loose slab edges — then hold the breakers until 8:00 and re-brief the supervisor.
options.feedback: Every extra minute is a continuing breach, and a part-broken bay can be made safe in minutes without breaking. It also tells the workforce the hours flex under programme pressure — the bay waits; your credibility with the authority doesn't come back as easily.

options.text: Explain to the office manager that the project is three weeks behind and early breaking is unavoidable for a fortnight, offer to avoid her conference call times, and ask her to call you directly rather than the council next time.
options.feedback: Announcing your intention to keep breaching the agreed hours — and asking her not to tell the council — is an invitation for the authority to serve notice, after which they set your hours, not you.
options.consequence: The office manager passed her call notes to environmental health; the council served a notice restricting noisy works to shorter hours for the rest of the project.

options.text: Let the gang carry on to 8:00 — it's forty minutes, the council doesn't inspect before nine, and one complaint against a three-week delay won't go anywhere — then call the office back mid-morning.
options.feedback: Deliberately breaching agreed noise hours is a fast route to formal action that can stop all noisy works on the council's terms — and the complaint log is evidence.
options.criticalFailure: Knowingly continued noisy works in breach of agreed hours
options.consequence: Environmental health was already logging repeat complaints; the council prosecuted for breach of the consent conditions, and the client's name featured in the local press.

eventPool.topic: Noise consent hours and neighbour response
eventPool.learningNote: Hours agreed with the local authority are operating conditions: brief them, police them, and treat any breach as an incident with an investigation and a personal response to the complainant. Losing the authority's trust means losing control of your own working hours.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: A shopper complains at the gate that dust from your site is drifting over the gantry onto the footpath, and you find an operative on the second lift dry-cutting blockwork with no water suppression and his mask hanging round his neck.

options.text: Stop the cutting now; restart only with water suppression or on-tool extraction and face-fit-tested RPE; find out how a dry cut began at the public edge; answer the shopper, log the complaint and re-brief silica controls.
options.feedback: Correct. This is a health exposure for the operative and a nuisance and reputational incident at the boundary in one. Control at source first, protect the person, then fix the supervision gap that let it start dry.

options.text: Tell the operative to put his FFP3 mask on, wet the cut line with a hand sprayer for the remaining few cuts, and ask the scaffolder to add a second layer of debris netting on that lift to keep the dust off the footpath and the gantry below.
options.feedback: A mask over stubble with no face-fit, a hand sprayer and an extra net layer don't control silica from a dry disc cutter — and the dust keeps rolling over the gantry onto the public while he finishes.
options.consequence: Dust kept drifting onto the footpath for another hour; the shopper complained to the council and HSE, and a later inspection found no face-fit records for the cutting gang.

options.text: Stop cutting on the scaffold and move the task to a bench in the rear yard, away from the footpath and the shoppers, with the operative reminded to wear his mask and the yard gate kept shut.
options.feedback: That manages the complaint, not the hazard — the operative is still breathing silica, and the yard is next to the neighbours' windows. Suppression and extraction fix both locations.

options.text: Apologise to the shopper, offer to pay for any cleaning, and let the operative finish — dust is unavoidable on a refurbishment, the cuts are nearly done, and the netting holds most of it back.
options.feedback: There is no safe exposure to respirable silica, and visible dust crossing your boundary onto the public is precisely what brings inspectors to refurbishment sites.
options.criticalFailure: Dry cutting continued without suppression or effective RPE
options.consequence: HSE followed up the complaint, found repeated dry cutting at the public edge with no suppression or face-fit records, and served an improvement notice with fee for intervention.

eventPool.topic: Silica dust — control at source and the public boundary
eventPool.learningNote: Cutting is controlled at source — water suppression or on-tool extraction — with face-fitted RPE as backup, never as the plan. Visible dust leaving site is both a health failure and an enforcement magnet: treat any dry-cutting discovery as a stop-and-fix, not a reminder.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: You find that the demolition gang has removed one prop from the designed propping layout on the first floor to get the skid-steer through an opening, and stood it against the wall 'to go back after the machine's through'.

options.text: Clear the bays above and below, stop plant on that slab, have the TWC and propping designer assess and direct reinstatement, verify it before reopening, and find out how the gang came to alter temporary works unapproved.
options.feedback: Correct. The layout is a designed structure — one prop out changes the load paths for everything around it, with a machine driving over the top. Exclusion, engineered reinstatement, verification, then fix the control failure.

options.text: Have the gang stand the prop back in its marked position and tighten it up, get the foreman to check it against the propping drawing, and carry on — it was out for twenty minutes with the machine working at the far end of the slab.
options.feedback: Unsafe. A prop re-stood by the gang that shouldn't have touched it, and checked by their own foreman, is unverified against the design — it may be carrying nothing, and the slab was loaded by plant while the layout was broken.
options.criticalFailure: Unauthorised propping alteration reinstated without engineering verification
options.consequence: The re-stood prop carried no load; when the skid-steer crossed back, the slab cracked and sagged onto the floor below — a RIDDOR dangerous occurrence — and HSE served a prohibition notice.

options.text: Log the alteration for the TWC's walk-round on Friday, tell the gang in writing never to touch the props again, and keep the machine working well away from the gap in the layout until then.
options.feedback: Four more days of plant and people on a slab whose propping is in an unknown state. Temporary works alterations are a now problem for the TWC and the designer, not a Friday agenda item.
options.consequence: Before Friday's walk-round the slab over the missing prop showed a visible crack; the bays were evacuated and the floor was out of use for a week while the designer reassessed.

options.text: Take the skid-steer off the slab straight away as a precaution, call the TWC to come and assess the layout, and let the gang carry on with hand demolition in those bays while you wait for him.
options.feedback: Taking the plant load off helps, but people are still working around propping in an unverified state — the exclusion and the engineering assessment come before any work resumes there.

eventPool.topic: Temporary works — unauthorised alteration of propping
eventPool.learningNote: Nobody alters propping except under the TWC's control, to the designer's direction — and reinstatement needs verification, not good intentions. If gangs are moving props to get plant through, the design didn't allow for the plant route: fix that through the TWC, not around them.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: A refuse lorry servicing the shops clips a leg of the pavement gantry at the kerb line. The structure looks straight from the ground, the driver wants to exchange details and go, and shoppers are walking under the gantry now.

options.text: Close and divert the footpath under the gantry now, with the authority as needed; have the TWC and gantry designer inspect the struck leg and connections before reopening; record the strike and the driver's details; review kerb protection.
options.feedback: Correct. A struck support is unverified structure with the public beneath it — 'looks straight' is not an assessment. Close, inspect to the design, then reopen; and if a strike was possible, the impact protection needs reviewing.

options.text: Walk the gantry deck and check the struck leg for plumb with a spirit level; if nothing has visibly shifted, keep the footpath open and ask the scaffold contractor to inspect it on their next visit.
options.feedback: Impact damage hides in connections, couplers and base details that a deck walk and a level can't see. Every shopper passing underneath is trusting a structure nobody qualified has verified since the strike.
options.consequence: The struck leg's base had sheared a fixing; the deck settled overnight onto the kerb-side ledger and the footpath was closed for three days for an engineered repair.

options.text: Cone off the struck leg and the kerb-side half of the footpath, keep pedestrians walking on the building-line side under the gantry, and call the scaffold contractor's inspector out this morning.
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but the gantry is one structure — if the impacted leg has shed load, the deck above the walking route is relying on members now carrying loads they weren't checked for.

options.text: Take the driver's and his company's details for the insurance claim and keep the footpath open — the leg still looks plumb from the ground, gantries are built to take knocks at the kerb, and closing it would push shoppers out into the busy road.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Normalising strikes on the structure protecting the public is how a later, harder strike finds a weakened gantry. Every impact gets an engineering check — that is the deal that lets you build over a footpath.
options.criticalFailure: Public allowed under gantry after vehicle strike without engineering inspection
options.consequence: A later, heavier strike buckled the already damaged leg; a section of deck dropped onto the kerb beside pedestrians — a RIDDOR dangerous occurrence and an HSE prohibition notice.

eventPool.learningNote: Any impact on a structure over the public means: exclude beneath, competent inspection against the design before reuse, record and report, and review the protection that let the vehicle reach it. Public protection structures get zero benefit of the doubt.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: With skips backing up in the yard, a haulier who has 'worked this street for years' offers same-day muck-away at two-thirds of your contracted rate, cash-friendly. He can't produce a waste carrier registration — 'the office has all that'.

options.text: Decline until the paperwork exists: check his carrier registration on the public register and the receiving site's permit, and only then consider him — meanwhile clear the backlog with your contracted carrier and more collections.
options.feedback: Correct. Duty of care means knowing who carries your waste and where it lands. Unverifiable carrier plus cash price usually equals a gateway to fly-tipping — with your transfer note, or none at all, in the load.

options.text: Use him for the clean brick and concrete arisings only — inert waste carries the lowest environmental risk — and keep the mixed and hazardous streams with the contracted carrier, with a signed transfer note for every load that leaves.
options.feedback: Inert waste is fly-tipped constantly — in gateways, lay-bys and fields — and the duty of care applies to every load regardless of what it is, starting with a verified carrier. Your name traces back with it.
options.consequence: Two of his loads of brick rubble were tipped in a field gateway outside the city; the council traced the project's transfer note and opened a duty-of-care investigation.

options.text: Take his details and vehicle registration, let him run one load of mixed waste today on a transfer note while his office sends the registration over, and hold any further loads until it arrives.
options.feedback: Once the load leaves, you have transferred waste to an unverified carrier — if it surfaces in a field gateway, the paper trail ends at your site and the offence is yours to answer.
options.criticalFailure: Waste transferred to an unverified carrier
options.consequence: The load was dumped in a lay-by; the transfer note led investigators to the site, and the principal contractor was prosecuted for breaching its waste duty of care.

options.text: Decline him, and absorb the backlog by compacting the full skips with the excavator bucket and topping them up until the contracted carrier's next scheduled run on Monday.
options.feedback: Declining is right and it keeps the waste legal, but compacting and overfilling builds a fire load and overloading problem in a tiny yard next to occupied premises — the real fix is collection frequency, which is a phone call.

eventPool.topic: Waste duty of care — carrier verification
eventPool.learningNote: Before any waste leaves site: carrier registration verified (the public register takes two minutes), destination permitted, transfer or consignment note completed and kept. A price that's too good is usually priced without the landfill gate fee — which tells you where the load is really going.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: An HSE inspector arrives unannounced after a complaint from a neighbouring office. She finds the pavement gantry deck stacked with strip-out waste well beyond its notice-boarded load limit, serves a prohibition notice on use of the gantry loading area, and tells you HSE will be recovering its costs.

options.text: Stop using the gantry area now, clear the load under TWC control, cooperate with the inspector, find out why the load limit was breached, brief the workforce and your employer, and resume only when remedied and re-checked.
options.feedback: Correct. A prohibition notice stops the activity immediately because of a risk of serious personal injury — here, to the public below. Comply, remedy, verify, and fix the system that let the overloading happen. Expect a fee-for-intervention invoice: where there is a material breach, HSE recovers its costs from the duty holder.

options.text: Comply with the notice and have the gantry cleared today, then write to the inspector's manager explaining that the load was short-term, the deck was still within its ultimate capacity, and the notice should be withdrawn at once.
options.feedback: You've avoided the offence but kept the failure. Overloading a public gantry is a structural near miss over the public — arguing about capacity treats the symptom and leaves the loading discipline and TW supervision unfixed.

options.text: Lodge an appeal with the employment tribunal straight away and keep using the gantry at half its notice-boarded load while the appeal is heard, with a banksman controlling what goes up.
options.feedback: A prohibition notice normally stays in force while an appeal is heard — appealing does not suspend it. Using the gantry meanwhile, at any load, risks prosecution for contravening the notice.
options.consequence: The tribunal declined to suspend the notice and HSE warned that further use would be prosecuted; the gantry stood idle through the appeal and the strip waste backlog grew.

options.text: Keep the gantry in use with the loading reduced — head office's legal team will challenge the notice, and stopping the gantry would leave the strip waste with nowhere to go.
options.feedback: Contravening a prohibition notice is a serious criminal offence in its own right — unlimited fines and potential imprisonment — separate from the underlying breach. And the risk to the public below the gantry is still live.
options.criticalFailure: Continued a prohibited activity in defiance of an enforcement notice
options.consequence: HSE returned, found the gantry in use and referred the contravention for prosecution; the company was heavily fined and the client withdrew the next phase of work.

eventPool.topic: Enforcement — improvement and prohibition notices, fee for intervention
eventPool.learningNote: Know the difference: an improvement notice requires a contravention to be fixed within a set time; a prohibition notice stops an activity that risks serious personal injury — usually with immediate effect — until it is remedied. Appeals go to a tribunal, but a prohibition notice normally stays in force meanwhile. Contravening either notice is itself an offence carrying unlimited fines and possible imprisonment, and HSE recovers its costs (fee for intervention) where there is a material breach.

modelAnswerNotes: Refurbishment and demolition asbestos survey and structural appraisal obtained before any strip or demolition planning; no intrusive work ahead of survey coverage.

Duty holders appointed in writing; F10 notified and displayed; demolition planned in writing by competent people; HSE-licensed asbestos contractor and engineered-demolition-capable contractor verified before appointment.
CPP proportionate and live, covering asbestos sequence, demolition, temporary works, fire in the stripped building and the public interface — in place before the phase started.

Site set-up: gantry and hoarding protecting the footpath; marshalled gate on the shared rear lane with booked deliveries; welfare stacked in the yard or established in the building; gas cage external; skips segregated in the yard, never in the lane; exclusion zone on the annexe; dust suppression at source.

Sequence protected people: asbestos removal with independent four-stage clearance area by area before strip; strip before machine demolition; nobody inside the exclusion zone with the machine working.

TWC appointed with stop-work authority; ten-item register with flank wall retention at cat 3 and propping, gantry and plant back-propping at cat 2 — all with hard hold points; movement monitoring with trigger levels and named escalation.
Permits: hot works, daily demolition authorisation, load/strike, asbestos clearance re-entry gate, services isolation and lifting — no dig or confined space permits padding the system.
Inspections: scaffold 7-day and after weather; gantry and hoarding after storms and strikes; monitoring read to schedule; thorough-examination certificates checked at the gate.
Fire controlled through the strip: daily waste removal, permit-controlled hot works with fire watch, temporary alarm and maintained escape routes, joint arrangements with the neighbours.

Environment: segregated waste with consignment notes for hazardous streams and verified carriers; noise consent hours agreed with the authority and policed; noise, vibration and dust monitored with trigger levels; neighbours told before disruptive works, complaints answered and closed.

Events handled by stop–exclude–get the engineer/analyst–fix the system: cracks stopped demolition, struck gantry closed the footpath, torn sheeting triggered after-weather inspection, finds triggered stop-seal-sample.

Handover: updated asbestos register (removed and retained ACMs with certificates), structural as-builts and residual risks into the H&S file; gantry and scaffold strike planned as controlled temporary works with footpath reinstatement agreed.
